messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Somchai was 69 and had spent most of his working life as a plumber, the kind of man who was used to crawling under houses, checking tight spaces, and trusting his hands to solve problems. He had emigrated from Southeast Asia decades earlier, built a quiet life in America, and now lived with his wife in a small house that he had carefully arranged so he could see the front door and the hallway from where he sat. It was in that ordinary domestic setting, and at work in basements and mechanical rooms, that the old fear kept finding him. He had been held captive years ago, and he spoke of it reluctantly, as if the words themselves might pull him back there. When he was unexpectedly alone with other men, or when a male coworker stepped too close in a narrow crawl space, his body would seize up before he could think. A wave of nausea could rise so quickly that he had to stop what he was doing, and a sharp pain in his neck would follow, making him stiff and watchful. Those moments did not just remind him of the captivity; they seemed to carry the same menace, and Somchai had come to brace himself by planning an escape route before entering nearly any unfamiliar place, a habit that had become automatic over the years. He also avoided dates tied to the event, quietly withdrawing around anniversaries, and he described detaching himself from the memories as though he could place them at a distance and keep functioning.

What Somchai remembered was not a story he could tell in a straight line. He said the memories came back like a film that played over and over, each return feeling as vivid as the first time. When he tried to explain what happened, he lost the thread and could not finish; the details seemed to break apart in his mouth, and he knew what happened without being able to find the words. That very failure to speak made the memory feel more powerful, not less, because the event remained uncontained and alive in his mind. He could picture being confined with men he did not know, listening for footsteps, waiting for the next movement, and the images would cycle through his head until his stomach tightened and his neck went rigid. The replaying scenes made him dread not only the memory itself but anything that resembled it. A sudden motion from a man walking behind him in a supply store, a maintenance worker appearing in a doorway, even standing too close to another man in a parking lot could set him on edge immediately. The memory kept supplying these cues, and the cues kept dragging the memory back.

In response, Somchai had built a life around keeping the past at a distance, but the strategies had begun to narrow his world. He detached himself from the memories whenever they surfaced, telling himself not to dwell on them, yet the more he pushed them away the more they seemed to come back in fragments. He planned exits before entering restaurants, clinics, and hardware stores, and he monitored the men around him with a vigilance that left little room for comfort. He had become on guard even inside his own home, checking the doors more than once and feeling his shoulders tense whenever he heard footsteps in the hall. The habit of avoiding anniversaries and slipping away from reminders did ease him for a moment, but it also kept the memory uncrossed and unspoken, so that when it returned it felt just as raw. At work, if he had to enter a cramped basement with another man, he would feel the old alertness surge and would calculate where he could move if he needed to get out quickly. His wife had noticed that he sat closer to the wall at gatherings and rarely stayed long. He no longer volunteered for some jobs that used to be routine, and he found himself making excuses to leave situations that involved being trapped in a space with men he did not know well.

By the time he sought help, Somchai was tired of living as if danger could appear at any moment. The fear was not only in his head; it came with nausea, neck pain, and a jolt through his whole body whenever something resembled the old captivity, and those reactions convinced him that he was still not safe. He had begun to worry that the memories and the constant guarding were wearing him down and making him less present with his wife and less confident at work. What brought him in was the sense that his world was shrinking around these reactions, and what he feared most was that he would never be able to talk about what happened clearly enough to make it feel over, or to stand in a room with other men without his body telling him he was back in that place again.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows reminders and cues, but it does not clearly state that these triggers drive Somchai’s safety behaviors or avoidance as a causal response in the same paragraph.
The vignette describes intrusive memories, but it does not explicitly show the memories causing the use of maladaptive coping or avoidance behaviors in the same paragraph.
It states that he detaches, plans exits, and avoids reminders, but it does not clearly convey that these maladaptive strategies lead to more memory intrusions or fragmentation.
It describes safety behaviors and vigilance, but it does not clearly state that these strategies themselves increase his sense of threat or danger in a causal way.
